extracted.intended_audience: graduate and advanced undergraduate students studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's Math 216 / The Rising Sea)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, constructions, and key structural results about effective Cartier divisors, invertible (line) bundles, quasicoherent sheaves on Proj of a graded ring, global generation/base-point-freeness, Serre's Theorem A, and pushforwards/pullbacks of quasicoherent sheaves. Includes exercises, examples, and precise local descriptions used to recognise/construct these objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Cartier divisor (local criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed subscheme D whose ideal sheaf I_D is an invertible sheaf (equivalently, locally cut out by a single equation that is not a zerodivisor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On an affine trivializing open Spec A with I ≅ A, I is generated by a single element a; multiplication by a is injective so a is not a zerodivisor. In the locally Noetherian case this is restated: D is locally cut out by a single equation not vanishing at any associated point of X. (Exercise 14.3.A: a is unique up to multiplication by an invertible function.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Invertible sheaf associated to an effective Cartier divisor (O(D))
rubrics_metrics.description: For an effective Cartier divisor D with ideal sheaf I_D, the invertible sheaf O(D) is defined to be the dual I_D^∨ (the ideal sheaf I_D is sometimes denoted O(-D)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a canonical section s_D of O(D) obtained by tensoring 0 → I_D → O_X → O_D → 0 with I_D^∨; this section cuts out D (Exercise 14.3.B). The dual choice (rather than I_D itself) is justified by Exercise 14.3.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section ↔ effective Cartier divisor correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction D ↦ (O(D), s_D) is reversible: if L is an invertible sheaf and s a section that is locally not a zerodivisor, then s = 0 cuts out an effective Cartier divisor D and O(D) ≅ L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make precise what 'locally not a zerodivisor' means (in the locally Noetherian case: s does not vanish at any associated point), see Exercise 14.3.C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of Cartier divisors and tensor/product rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If I and J are invertible ideal sheaves corresponding to effective Cartier divisors D and D', then the product ideal I·J is invertible and corresponds to the Cartier divisor D + D'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On afﬁnes define product of ideal sheaves by product of ideals; verify (IJ)_f = I_f J_f in localizations. Verify O(D + D') ≅ O(D) ⊗ O(D') (Exercise 14.3.D). Effective Cartier divisors form an abelian semigroup; there is a semigroup map to invertible sheaves with sections (and hence to Picard group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation of invertible sheaves via differences of effective Cartier divisors
rubrics_metrics.description: Many invertible sheaves arise as differences of two effective Cartier divisors; on regular or factorial schemes (and often for finite-type k-schemes, projective schemes, etc.) every invertible sheaf can be so described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fails in general (Kleiman's example). References: Proposition 14.2.10, Auslander–Buchsbaum Theorem 12.8.5, [Gr–EGA], Exercise 16.6.F for projective case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proj construction (projective A-scheme from graded ring)
rubrics_metrics.description: A projective A-scheme is produced from a Z_{6gt;=0}-graded ring S_• with S_0 = A and S_+ a finitely generated ideal; the scheme is Proj S_•.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume S_• is finitely generated over A; many later constructions (O(n), twists, etc.) are defined when S_• is generated in degree 1 (or after replacing by a Veronese subring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasicoherent sheaf from graded module (~ construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a Z-graded S_•-module M_•, define a quasicoherent sheaf ~M_• on Proj S_• by setting on D(f) (for homogeneous f of positive degree) the module ((M_•)_f)_0 (the degree-0 part of the localization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These local descriptions glue via obvious restriction maps to give a quasicoherent sheaf; this defines a functor ~ from graded S_•-modules to QCoh(Proj S_•). Exercises: identify stalks (15.1.A), check exactness of ~ (15.1.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness and limitations of the ~ functor
rubrics_metrics.description: The ~ functor from graded S_•-modules to quasicoherent sheaves is exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, ~ is not an equivalence of categories: different graded modules can give the same sheaf (Exercise 15.1.C); agreement in high degrees produces same sheaf in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree shift / twisting of graded modules and sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: For a graded module M_• define M(n)_m := M_{n+m}; the associated sheaf satisfies #M(n)_• ≅ #M_•(n). Define O(1) = #S(1) and O(n) = O(1)^{6otimes n}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If S_• is generated in degree 1 then O(n) is an invertible sheaf (Exercise 15.2.B). Also O(m+n) ≅ O(m) ⊗ O(n) (Exercise 15.2.D). If S_• is not generated in degree 1, pass to a Veronese subring (Remark 15.2.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Globally generated (generated by global sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasicoherent sheaf F on X is globally generated if there is a surjection O_X^{6oplus I} → F (i.e., the images of global sections generate each stalk). Finite global generation means I can be taken finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent local formulations: F is globally generated at p iff O_X^{6oplus I}_p → F_p is surjective; for finite type F on quasicompact X, global generation at closed points implies global generation everywhere (15.3.C, 15.3.D). For affine schemes every quasicoherent sheaf is globally generated (15.3.A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Base locus and base-point-free (for line bundles and linear series)
rubrics_metrics.description: For invertible sheaf L, the base locus is the (closed) set of points where all global sections vanish; L is base-point-free iff base locus is empty (equivalently L globally generated). For a linear series V ⊂ Γ(X,L), base-points are points where every element of V vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base-point-free locus is open. Tensor of two base-point-free line bundles is base-point-free (15.3.4, 15.3.B). n+1 sections of L with no common zeros define a morphism X → P^n (15.3.F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear series / complete linear series
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear series on a k-scheme X is a finite-dimensional k-vector space V (often a subspace of Γ(X,L)), an invertible sheaf L, and a linear map λ: V ⊗ O_X → L; if λ is an isomorphism onto Γ(X,L) it's the complete linear series |L|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An (n+1)-dimensional base-point-free linear series defines a morphism to P^n whose domain is the base-point-free locus (15.3.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's Theorem A (finite global generation after twisting)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S_• is generated in degree 1 and finitely generated over A = S_0, then for any finite-type quasicoherent sheaf F on Proj S_• there exists n_0 such that for all n ≥ n_0, F(n) is finitely globally generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Theorem 15.3.8; it is used to prove Theorem 15.3.1 (presentation by sums of O(-n)). A proof is deferred (Theorem 16.6.2 will give a consequence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of coherent sheaves by line bundles (Theorem 15.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any finite-type sheaf F on Proj S_• admits a surjection from a finite direct sum of twists of O, i.e. ⊕_{finite} O(-n_i) → F → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: one can build (possibly infinite) resolutions of F by sums of line bundles; Hilbert Syzygy Theorem asserts finiteness of such resolutions on P^n_k (length ≤ n) in that context (15.3.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Γ_• functor (graded global sections) and saturation map
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Γ_n(F):= Γ(Proj S_•, F(n)), giving a graded S_•-module Γ_•(F). For a graded module M_• there is a natural saturation map M_• → Γ_•(~M_•).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Γ_• is a functor QCoh(Proj S_•) → graded S_•-modules (15.4.B, 15.4.E). The saturation map need not be injective/surjective in general (15.4.D), but for finitely generated M_• over a field it is an isomorphism in large degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjunction and recovery: ~ and Γ_• are adjoint; QCoh arises from graded modules
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural isomorphism #Γ_•(F) ≅ F, and the functors ~ and Γ_• form an adjoint pair; every quasicoherent sheaf on a projective A-scheme arises from the ~ construction (after saturation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every closed subscheme of Proj S_• arises from a homogeneous graded ideal I_• (Exercise 15.4.H). Proj of Γ_•(S_•) recovers the saturated projective scheme with its O(1) (15.4.J, 15.4.K).

rubrics_metrics.name: Saturated graded modules and uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: For each quasicoherent sheaf there is a 'best' (saturated) graded module M_• whose ~ is that sheaf; the saturation functor M_• ↦ M_•^{sat} is idempotent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different graded modules can give the same sheaf, but saturated modules are canonical representatives. There is a bijection between saturated quasicoherent sheaves of ideals and closed subschemes of Proj S_• (15.4.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushforward of quasicoherent sheaves (affine and general cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: Spec A → Spec B is a morphism of affine schemes and M is an A-module corresponding to a quasicoherent sheaf, then π_* corresponds to the module viewed as a B-module via restriction (Exercise 16.2.A). In general, if π: X → Y is quasicompact and quasiseparated and F is quasicoherent on X, then π_*F is quasicoherent (Theorem 16.2.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For affine morphisms π_*: QCoh_X → QCoh_Y is exact (16.2.B). Coherent sheaves need not push forward to coherent sheaves in general (example: structure morphism A^1_k → Spec k), but under finite morphisms of Noetherian schemes or proper/projective morphisms pushforwards of coherent sheaves are coherent (16.2.C and later Theorem 18.9.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pullback of quasicoherent sheaves (local tensor description)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π: X → Y and a quasicoherent sheaf G on Y, locally on affine opens Spec A ⊂ X lying over Spec B ⊂ Y with G|_{Spec B} corresponding to the B-module N, one has Γ(Spec A, π^*G) = N ⊗_B A; in other words the pullback locally corresponds to base change via tensor product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three perspectives: (a) describe via affines and glue, (b) define by universal property and check locality, (c) define as the standard ringed-space pullback (all agree and produce a quasicoherent sheaf). Examples: restriction to open immersion, fiber at a point, and pulling back vector bundles via transition matrices (16.3). Exercises 16.3.2–16.3.7 guide the construction and glueing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies and checks for defining pullback
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining π^*G one may (a) construct on affine covers by the tensor formula and glue, (b) use the universal property to characterise π^*, (c) use the ringed-space definition; verify the pullback is quasicoherent by checking affine-local descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When handling restrictions to π^{-1}(Spec B) one defines φ = π|_{π^{-1}(Spec B)} and constructs φ^*(G|_{Spec B}) by the tensor formula on each distinguished open D(f). Show compatibility and glue to π^*G (see 16.3.2–16.3.3).
